newsitem.title: INDIA: India shipping faces rough weather, seeks relief.
newsitem.headline: India shipping faces rough weather, seeks relief.

text.p: Indian shipowners are little better off despite six years of burgeoning trade volumes due to economic liberalisation, while foreign rivals, operating out of tax havens, have filled their holds with the extra cargo.

"India must realise that globally shipping is a competitive business. You must provide a level playing field to compete. Right now things are unequal on my own turf," B.L.Mehta, president of the Indian National Shipowners' Association, said.
"Internationally, the shipping industry survives essentially on tax-free regimes. Nearly 75 percent of it does not pay taxes," Mehta told Reuters.

The financial burdens imposed by taxes and high interest rates handicapped domestic shipping lines while their freer competitors streamed into Indian ports hungry for a share of the growth in cargo that followed reforms begun in 1991.
According to INSA, domestic shipping's share of India's foreign trade fell steadily to about 25 percent by 1995/96 (April/March) since 1987/88 when it peaked to 41 percent.
"Since 1985 onwards we have been moving around 7.0 million grt (gross registered tonnage). In 17 years' time we have added only one million tonnes. It's nothing," Mehta said.
He said while India's shipping tonnage stagnated, its overseas trade - exports and imports - grew at an average annual rate of 18 percent.
Indian shipping companies have also faced a sea-change in trading patterns following the break-up of the Soviet Union in 1991, which reduced bilateral trade with the eastern bloc.
Shipowners said foreign firms had also entered India's coastal trade, previously reserved for local companies but thrown open by reforms.

Mehta said half the world's shipping had grouped itself under the banner of flags of convenience (FOC), offered by countries like Liberia, Honduras, Singapore and Hong Kong. Most rich nations were flagging off their ships under FOC, where they can avoid paying corporate tax, he said.
Mehta said shipping lines operating from tax havens raised resources internally and bought ships more cheaply because of better credit terms.
"My competitor out there is raising capital at 7.0 percent against my 17 percent. How can I compete?," Mehta said, referring to higher interest rates in India.
At the end of April 1997, India's total shipping tonnage stood at 6.88 million grt. "We are scrapping more tonnage than we are adding," INSA chief executive B.V. Neelkund said.
An expansion plan seeks to add 2.0 million grt of fresh tonnage and replace 1.7 million in the next five years to take the total tonnage to 9.0 million.
The cost of acquiring additional fleet has been estimated at 150 billion rupees ($4.2 billion), 30 percent of which is to come from equity and the rest through borrowing.
INSA has pleaded for tax and duty reliefs and an annual allocation of $300 million for commercial borrowings for shipping. A response from the finance ministry is yet to come.
Mehta said shipping was far down the government's list of priorities for receiving finances while fiscal benefits available in the past had been withdrawn.
"This attitude has stifled investment," he said. "No doubt, there's a shipping policy. But it's standing on its head."
To add more woes, dry bulk cargo freight rates have fallen nearly 20 percent on Baltic Freight Index since December, and industry sources see little cheer on the horizon.
"In a cyclical industry like shipping, if you are paying taxes out of your profits in good years, in the downswing period you make no money at all," INSA's Mehta said.
"It looks to me, in five years' time there will be no national shipping," he added. ($1.00 = 35.8 rupees)
